speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO HEADING OF REPORT IN MONTREAL "GAZETTE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a matter of personal privilege I wish to point out that there is carried in the Montreal Gazette of this morning a report which bears the headline: "Ships carried war materiel to China-P.M." The report is a Canadian Press report, and it is an accurate report of the discussions which took place in this house yesterday, but the headline would convey to many a quite erroneous impression. "War materiel" is taken by many to mean munitions, supplies or equipment for armed forces. The report contains this paragraph, which is correct:
Mr. St. Laurent said the reason the ships carried to China materials Canada herself now bans for export to Red countries was that the materials were not placed on Britain's banned list until a few days ago. Now the British and Canadian lists were virtually the same.
It would be most unfortunate if this headline conveyed the impression that I was indicating to the house that Britain allowed "war materiel" to be carried to communist China. For a great many there is a substantial difference between what are classified as strategic materials and what is described as "war materiel". I was speaking of the items on our list of strategic materials which, up to some days ago, was more restrictive than that of Britain. But I certainly did not wish to imply that the British authorities were allowing "war materiel" to be carried to communist China.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS FOR MAKING REFUNDS
speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Since this is the last day of the session may I be permitted to preface my remarks, sir, with a few explanatory words?-because this is a matter that affects many thousands of people across the country. Beginning on Monday, deductions of income tax will be made at the source without regard to the proper allowances to which the taxpayer would be entitled. Will the department arrange, as soon as possible after proof has been given as to the proper deductions to which the taxpayer would be entitled, to make the necessary refund? Otherwise the labouring man and the salaried man will have paid far more income tax than they should, and the money to which they are entitled by way of refund will be held for a considerable time.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS FOR MAKING REFUNDS
speechtext:
On June 18, when discussing section 15 of the Income Tax Act, I made a statement on the withholding tax, and I should like to read the last paragraph of it, which I think on consideration is as fair and explicit an answer as I can make to the question which my hon. friend has asked, and of which he has given me notice. I said, as reported at page 4246 of Hansard:
Finally, I should add that in those cases where the incidence of intermittent employment, charitable donations, or unusual medical expenses, brings about over-deductions of tax, refunds can and will be made within a very short time after the taxpayer files his annual return. This year, for example, all district offices had processed refunds within two to four weeks after the receipt of the returns. If the taxpayer will file his return promptly, the department will see to it that he gets his cheque with all possible dispatch.
I admit that there has been some delay in some instances, perhaps, because the practice is that we have to match what are called T4 slips-that is, the slips that come from the employer, in which he indicates the

Inquiries of the Ministry amount of money that has been paid to the employee and the deductions that have been made.
If the taxpayer will make his return any time after January 1 for the year preceding, and we have the T4 returns from the employer, I will guarantee that refunds will be made very promptly, and following our practice that has been done within two to four weeks of the receipt of the return.
As I stated yesterday on the estimates, all, or practically all, the refunds for the year 1950 have been made as of the middle of June. That is a condition that has never before obtained in the department.
One of the causes of delay has been the complaint-I will admit this-by some employers that they did not have the T4 forms as early as they would have liked. That is one of the matters that we can attend to this year; I will see to it that they have them early in January, and refunds will be made with great promptness.
I might say to the hon. gentleman that there is the other side of it, too; there are cases in which the payment is not enough, where individuals have earned income from other sources than salary or wages, and the amount of earned income other than salary or wages last year was in excess of the combined medical bills and charitable donations. However, that has nothing to do with it. It is just to show that there is another side to the case. In these instances we have to make an extra collection of tax; but we will continue to see to it that refunds are made as promptly as it is possible to make them.
The taxpayer has a right, and is invited, to make his return early in the year. If he does that, and we have the matching T4 form, we shall be able to make his refund accordingly.

speechtext: I thank the minister for that assurance, because a number of labouring men have written me in regard to it.

maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext:
The
other day I asked a question of the Minister of Transport about the probability of being able to take out of the western provinces all the 1950 wheat crop before the 1951 season begins. The Department of Transport stated that that was a matter for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I would now ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he is in a position to give this information.

It is of importance to western farmers who have much wheat on hand.
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Yes, Mr. Speaker, the movement of western grain from the prairies to market has been the cause of great concern since the opening of navigation. As hon. members know, the crop was very late last year, and the movement of the crop before the close of navigation was only about 50 per cent of normal. The movement to date is not such as would indicate that this crop will be moved from western Canada by the time the next crop is marketed. There will certainly be a considerable amount of grain at the lakehead, and the best we can hope is that the country elevators will be cleared.
Extraordinary efforts have been made to obtain additional lake tonnage, which is the bottleneck at the moment. The fact of the matter is that lake tonnage is not sufficient to move the quantity of wheat which must be moved by this summer and, in addition, take care of the minimum requirements for iron ore and other products which must also be moved. A conference is being held today, which is one of several conferences, through which it is hoped to divert additional tonnage from other services. Every effort is being made to get the grain forward, but one unfortunate result has been we have had to stop selling No. 6 wheat and feed wheat for the very reason that we cannot make deliveries within any reasonable time on account of transportation problems. That, I think, is the situation. If my hon. friend has any other questions I should be glad to answer them.

maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext:
Can the minister say
approximately what is the amount that will not be moved from the prairies? I am speaking particularly of the estimated amount in farm storage or in line elevators on the prairies. Then there is the other question arising out of the minister's statement. Approximately how much of the No. 6 wheat could be sold of which the wheat board has denied sale because transportation facilities are not available?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext:
Up to June 21 the railroads had moved 415 million bushels of grain out of country elevators in the western division. As of the same date, a total of 108 million bushels of grain remains in country elevators, and the railways still continue to carry on a reasonably large movement of grain right up to the end of the crop year. Considering present stocks of grain in country elevators, and the volume of grain which producers will market during the remainder of the crop year, it is expected that some 80 to 90 million bushels

of grain will remain in country positions at the end of the crop year. Those are the essential figures.

maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext: Does the minister know the capacity of the country elevators?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext: I do not remember. I used to have those figures in my mind, but I think it is about 200 million bushels.

maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext: Then there is the other question, in regard to the statement the minister made that No. 6 wheat, of which apparently there is a large amount on hand, cannot be sold because it cannot be moved. About how much No. 6 wheat is there in that condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext: The amount of No. 6 wheat and feed wheat remaining unsold, allowing for 20 million bushels carry-over, which is the normal requirement until the next crop is harvested, is about 60 to 65 million bushels. My hon. friend has asked how much could be sold if we could move it. I cannot answer that question, because we are not offering the wheat.

maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext: The minister said he could have sold it if it could have been moved.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: MOVEMENT OUT OF STORAGE AND FROM HEAD OF LAKES
speechtext: We could have sold more than we have to date. We have sold everything we have offered, but we offer it only if we are reasonably sure of getting it in a deliverable position at the time when it is required.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Defence Production. Is the minister aware of the growing unemployment in the automobile industry, and is there any statement he wishes to make before the house rises? Will he give the matter his active attention?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Of course the minister is giving that matter his active attention. As I said before, the situation at the present time is not clear as to what the actual employment is. I talked with General Motors officials a few days ago, and I was told that they do not expect employment to drop more than ten per cent from the peak employment figure-which peak employment was certainly abnormal. At the present time automobile factories in Windsor and vicinity are closed down, partly due to a strike in a parts
Supply-Veterans Affairs factory, and partly in order to readjust production schedules, the latter in the case of Ford.
Is that the Acme strike?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, the Acme strike. That strike is now settled, but it will take some time to get the product moving. Within the next week or two we should be able to assess the situation and see what the real unemployment situation is in the Windsor area. There is no lack of employment throughout industry in Ontario, as my hon. friend knows, if he sees the figures reported by the Department of Labour. In fact employment in the province is tighter than it has been for some years.
There will be no great difficulty, as I see it, in moving into other industries the men who may be displaced in the automobile industry. Most industries are short of productive manpower. All I can say to the house is that the department is giving close and careful attention to the situation, and believes that a remedy can be worked out within a reasonable time.

DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS Pensions and other benefits-
822. To provide financial assistance after the thirty-first day of May, 1951, in accordance with regulations to be made by the governor in council, to unemployable veterans who are in receipt of pensions under the Pension Act for a disability which is a factor contributing to their unemployability; such financial assistance to be exempt from income tax under the provisions of the Income Tax Act, $2,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, this matter was dealt with at considerable length in the committee on veterans affairs. As I was not a member of that committee, there are one or two references I should like to make to it.
I take the strongest objection to what appears to be a change in principle in the awarding of war pensions. Throughout the years the principle has been one of compensation for war injuries, or injuries received in service. This new term "unemployability" seems to incorporate the principle of establishing destitution-in other words, the means test-in relation to additions to the amount of a regular pension.
I think it is generally agreed throughout the country that some cost of living bonus should be added to war pensions, by reason of the tremendous increase in the cost of living since the last changes were made in pension levels. The present rate of pensions,

Supply-Veterans Affairs and also of war veterans allowances, is not in keeping with the needs of veterans, or indeed with the maintenance of that dignity to which the war veterans are entitled.
I do not often speak on veterans affairs, although from its inception I have been a member of the Canadian Legion. But I do protest most strenuously against what I believe is a departure from the true design and purpose of pensions legislation since 1919, and one that carries with it the possibility of establishing a principle which is contrary to the principles upon which war pensions should be paid.
In the last few weeks I have received petitions from various Canadian Legion branches, both in and outside my own province, protesting against this departure from true pension principles. I think every member in the House of Commons, however desirous he may be of maintaining economy, agrees that the present rate of pension should be increased in order, for the time being, to meet the changed conditions brought about by the high cost of living.
I speak not only as a member of the Legion, but as one who has received the representations to which I have referred. I am supported in the stand I take by the July, 1951, issue of The Legionary, which sets out in plain English the attitude taken by the Canadian Legion and its membership across this country.
I shall not read at length, but I shall put on record one or two brief quotations which set forth in epitome the views I hold on this important matter, as well as those of officials of the Canadian Legion. This editorial is entitled "In plain English," and states:
In plain English, then, the result of the committee's work was a very great disappointment to the Canadian Legion, as indeed it must have been to many members of the committee. To the great majority of war disability pensioners and their families who, in spite of the dreadful rise in living costs, will receive no increase whatever in their pensions at this time, the result is nothing less than a calamity.
Then it says:
In fact, judging by the shocking lack of sympathy displayed by certain government members and officials, this is almost certain to happen.
Then it refers to the calling of a fall session, when it is expected this matter will come up, and it continues:
. . . unless the cabinet is made to realize in the interval that the veteran body and the public and press of the dominion are really aroused over this glaring injustice.
Those are strong expressions, but they represent the considered opinion of representatives of the Canadian Legion, who speak

without partisanship but always with directness concerning the case of the veteran which that organization has served so well. It sums up the matter in these words:
As for the $2 million unemployability supplement, which the committee approved by an 18-10 vote, no one-least of all the employed pensioners-will begrudge for a moment the unfortunate veterans, who are completely unable to work, the supplementary allowance the government is going to give them. But, as the Legion's representatives pointed out again and again to the committee, the new principle being established through the introduction of this palliative is a humiliating and thoroughly undesirable one, being based on charitable compassion instead of proud right earned through the shedding of blood or impairment of health while fighting for our country's survival.
That language is stronger than anything else I have read in The Legionary. Throughout the years the Canadian Legion has served the Canadian people by the stand it has taken in the maintenance of all that is good and proper in our way of life. Someone might ask if I would vote against this. Certainly not, and it is simply begging the issue to ask that question. The unemployability supplement means that tens of thousands of veterans in this country who are unable to carry on but who none the less can take some employment are going to be denied the measure of fairness and consideration to which they are entitled.
I noticed recently that one of the ministers stated that over ninety per cent of the pensioners were employed. I do not know where those statistics were secured. When the minister was asked on what they were based, he stated that a spot-check had been made of 35,000 veterans. Personally I do not believe that check was general enough; for I know that in my province many pensionable veterans are becoming more and more unemployable, particularly those who served in the first war. The stand taken here is a parsimonious one having regard to the need of the veterans who for the most part are receiving pensions and who are depending on those pensions for a reasonable degree of sustenance.
While agreeing that this does touch the fringe of the problem, in touching the fringe it establishes a principle that is a denial of all the foundation principles of pensions legislation which have been established over the years. I protest against it, because I feel that service entitlement is no longer made the qualification for a pension, but rather that destitution and unemployability are being substituted in part so far as this supplement is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a word or two on the subject to which the hon. member for Lake Centre has referred. I was not able to serve this year

on the special committee because, as to numbers, membership on the committee was restricted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Just two less.

I do not know why the membership of the committee was so small, but certainly, it was not possible for all members who are veterans to serve on that committee. I am not going to take advantage of this opportunity to say everything that might have been said in the committee, because those who were on the special committee discussed this matter quite fully; but I do want to bring to the attention of the minister one or two matters which I was not able to bring before the committee.
The British Columbia command of the Canadian Legion were holding their provincial conference at the time this matter came before the special committee, and they sent in the strongest of protests against the introduction of the means test principle in connection with the unemployability supplement and the regulations the government are laying down prescribing the payment of that supplement. In addition I received a telegram-this was the subject of some comment earlier in the house-from the president of Branch No. 70 of the tubercular veterans section, Canadian Legion, Tranquille, British Columbia. A large tuberculosis sanitarium is operated there by the provincial government, and Branch No. 70 has a large number of members. These are the types of veterans who would be expected to receive the unemployability supplement provided for in this item. They are the very veterans who might be expected to benefit, but they go on record as being strongly opposed to the principle being laid down in the regulations covering the payment of this supplement. I should like to read the telegram as I received it:
We would like to go on record as protesting the apathetic approach of the Liberal government in dealing with the veterans pensions and problems. We protest most vigorously the charitable stigma which a pensioner is being made to feel. The problem besetting pensioned veterans today is adversely affecting the recruiting campaign and will continue to do so until the security promised veterans is forthcoming. It is with regret that we noted party politics rearing its ugly head in veterans affairs. This is indisputably shown in the vote taken in parliamentary committee of veterans affairs. Out of 31 members 20 are Liberals. Nineteen Liberals voted against veterans getting a fair break. This same political party was the one that promised the veterans security in their future. It is to be noted that the shameless disregard of the Liberals to their obligations is ignored. It is with deep concern that we noted that the government-
I think they meant to refer to the session.
-will be called to a halt without this legislation being rectified. This is against all principles of free
Supply-Veterans Affairs
enterprise. Normally if a person or assembly commits itself, it should fulfil its contract or resign. Needless to say we are disillusioned and disgusted with the Liberal government.
Copies sent to the following:	Mr. St. Laurent,
Mr. Lapointe, Mr. E. D. Fulton, General Pearkes, MP, Ottawa; also letters to editor, Vancouver Sun, editor, Vancouver Province, Mr Robinson, T.V.S. Secretary, Canadian Legion, Ottawa and provincial command.
James Athey
President, Branch 70, T.V.S.
That is the telegram about which I questioned the Prime Minister on an earlier occasion; I asked whether he had received it, and I was told at that time that it had been turned down by the Prime Minister's office. I received later word to the effect that arrangements were made by the branch to pay for the telegram so that the Prime Minister might actually see a copy, and in fact a copy was delivered to the Prime Minister's office after that had been arranged. Therefore the Prime Minister had received the telegram. I hope that the Minister of Veterans Affairs has received it, because the thing I wish to emphasize is that the tuberculous veterans, who above all might be expected to receive the benefit of the regulations for the unemployability supplement as they are now drafted, are, generally speaking, men of no private means, with nothing beyond their pensions, men whose position deserves the utmost sympathy and consideration from this house. Yet they are the very ones who send this vigorous protest against the principle of the system which is being introduced in this supplement. As they put it, "We protest most vigorously the charitable stigma which a pensioner is being made to feel".
I hope, since this is the last day of the session and it is not probable that any adjustment will be made at this time, that the minister will be moved, as a result of representations from the very people who would be expected to receive the supplement, to alter the regulations in the future and to eliminate from them this means test principle.

In view of the fact I spoke at some length on this item at the time we were discussing departmental administration, I have no intention of delaying the committee, but I should like to emphasize one point. First of all I should like to remind hon. members that there has been a substantial increase in the cost of living and in wage levels since 1948, and, owing to the fact that there has been no increase in the basic rate of pension since that time, disability pensioners today are under a severe handicap. This item provides assistance to a total of only approximately 6,000 disability pensioners out of a total of 162,000. I see the parliamentary assistant shaking his head. It is
4984	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs estimated that about 6,000 will benefit. It is possible that later on more will benefit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I was shaking my head because the hon. member said out of a potential of
162.000,	whereas he knows that under the regulations the potential is a maximum of
34.000.
But there are actually 162,000 disability pensioners.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It sounds worse that way.

Unfortunately under this item no pension will be given to a single veteran with a disability of less than thirty-five per cent or to a married veteran with a disability of less than forty-five per cent. Many members on the Liberal side have emphasized the fact that the purpose of the item is good, and will give assistance to those who are most in need. Unfortunately it does not do that, because today many veterans who are paid for a thirty-five per cent or forty-five per cent disability actually have a disability of one hundred per cent, but it cannot be shown that it is due to war service and they get no pension for it. Many of these men are in dire need and yet they will not be able to get any assistance under the provisions of this estimate. The veterans affairs committee recommended that the government increase the basic rate of pension, or at least give consideration to it. I should like to ask the minister whether or not the government has given any consideration to the recommendation of the committee for an increase in the basic rate of disability pension.

This week a bill was passed
increasing pensions for judges by twenty per cent to compensate for the increase in the cost of living since 1946. The cost of living has increased by sixteen per cent since the last increase was made in veterans pensions. So far as the veterans are concerned, the government has completely turned down the many requests made for an adequate increase in their pensions to enable them to maintain their standard of living in the same way as all other citizens of the country.
I believe it is impossible to reconcile the attitude and action of the government in these two matters. On the one hand they seem very worried that one class of citizens, the judges, should have an increase in their pensions and salaries so that they can maintain their standard of living and keep up with the rising cost of living. On the other hand they completely disregard the needs of a class of citizens who I think merit the greatest consideration, those whose service to the country has not been surpassed in any way by any other class of citizens.

I refer to our war veterans. I should like to hear what the minister has to say in explanation of the government's policy of giving one class of citizen, namely, the judges, a twenty per cent increase-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
-and on the other hand refusing an increase to war veterans.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member
may not refer to a previous debate, and we have had a previous debate on judges pensions and salaries.

I have put my question. I am sure that the minister and the government must have an explanation. It is a very important thing to our war veterans. I do not think any class of citizens has given greater service to the country than our war veterans. Why they should be treated in one way, while another class of citizens should be treated in quite a different way, is something that I and other members of the opposition find it impossible to understand. I should like to hear an explanation from the Minister of Veterans Affairs as to why he considers this is a fair deal for the veterans of the country. Could I have an answer, please?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was answered why while
you were electioneering.

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext: I certainly do not intend to go over the debate which took place on the Judges Act. A full explanation of the policy of the government was given at that time. I do not know whether my hon. friend was here, but I do not think it is proper to take up that matter in this debate. I think my hon. friend agrees with me, too.

Would	the	minister answer
my question, whether the government has given consideration to the recommendation of the committee?
I can certainly assure my hon. friend that all recommendations of the special committee on veterans affairs are being very closely studied and considered by the government.

Three or
four years ago I suggested that these pensions should be hooked to the cost of living index. I do not think we will ever arrive at a satisfactory solution of the problem until some plan of that kind is worked out. If and when it is worked out, it should be done with reference to the time when we had a real dollar in this country.

Hon. members to my right who have spoken in the last few minutes have emphasized the fact that this is the last day
LMr. Quelch.]

of the session, and that it was too bad a lot of things had not been done before the last day arrived. This does not necessarily have to be the last day. If every member gets to his feet and occupies the same amount of time as those who have spoken, this will not be the last day; there will be several more days.
I agree with the minister that this matter was before a committee for about five weeks, and thereafter there was a full-dress debate in the house which gave everyone an opportunity of expressing an opinion on government policy. I expressed mine, and it is on the record, both in the committee and in the house.
I rise at this time to correct something the member for Lake Centre put on the record. He said that the policy of the government in connection with this unemployable supplement was strongly condemned by the Legion, and that is correct. But he said that as a result of the work of that committee, this action was brought about.
The last thing I wanted to imply was that, Mr. Chairman.
The hon. member should look at the record.

It was a great committee, and it has done a magnificent job, so that is the last thing I wanted to imply. If there was the slightest implication of that, it certainly was not intended, nor could I conceive of the words being possible of that interpretation.
The hon. member was quoting an article from this month's issue of The Legionary, and if he will look at the record again he will see that that is correct.
Oh, the quotation from the article-I beg your pardon. I thought the hon. member said that I said that.

This vote in the supplementary estimates was placed in the hands of the committee so that there could be a general discussion of its implications. The veterans affairs committee could not accept or reject it, because that is the responsibility of the house. All the committee could do was to send the estimate back to the house, and the final vote on that $2 million is a vote of the house. We want to keep the record straight on that, because a year from now someone will be quoting the member for Lake Centre over the radio and saying: You were a member of the committee that brought it in. The committee could not accept or reject it, and could only discuss it and recommend that it be returned to the house for a vote. In the final analysis the vote is a vote of the House of Commons.

I am not going to say anything about the merits or demerits of his policy. My opinions are on the record, and I voted against it. The committee recommended further consideration of the matter of basic pensions.

There is one way in which the minister could deal effectively with this matter this morning. In response to a question that was asked, he indicated that he will, of course, give consideration to any recommendations that have been made. Nevertheless I would point out that these recommendations have now been in the hands of the government for some time. Without in any way referring directly to any particular piece of legislation that has been before this house, I would point out that since that time the government has established the principle of recognizing the need for meeting the increased cost of living on a percentage basis. If that applies in one case, it applies in the other. If there is one particular case in which any just provision should apply with more force than another, it is the case of the veteran. The highest obligation of this or any other government is to give adequate consideration to those who have offered the highest type of service that a man or a woman can give in support of the state.
It is not possible for the opposition to move an amendment that would increase this figure or affect the principle which applies to this figure. Nevertheless, the minister has received these recommendations; he has had time to consider them., and since in the other case the government has adopted a principle consistent with what is being urged by the opposition, I would ask the minister to dispose of this matter by giving us an undertaking that when we meet in October he will take the proper steps to introduce legislation that will provide for a uniform over-all percentage increase to the veterans consistent with the increased cost of living.

The leader of the opposition realizes that any such statement on my part would be an undertaking on behalf of the government. I do not believe he expects me at this moment to give an undertaking of that sort without consulting my colleagues in the cabinet. Such a decision would definitely be a question of government policy which would have to be decided by the government. Frankly I have no hesitation in saying that I cannot give such an undertaking at the present time. I did state that the recommendations of the committee, which included the subject matter mentioned by the leader of the opposition, had been put

Supply-Veterans Affairs before the government and will be considered by the government. If there is any change of policy, it will be announced by the government or by myself.

Naturally I recognized that a statement by the minister would be a statement on behalf of the government. Notwithstanding the fact adjournment may be expected fairly soon, I hope that this item may be allowed to stand while the minister consults with other members of the government. Since this matter was brought before us the government recognized the increased cost of living on a percentage basis in another case, so I do not think he should have much difficulty in getting the approval of the government. A statement on this principle at this time would greatly reassure the veterans during the next three months.

I note that most of the members who have spoken on this item have been veterans, but perhaps I may be allowed to say a few words because there were more enlistments per capita from my constituency during the first and second world wars than from any other constituency in Canada. We have, therefore, a great many pensioners and a great many unemployable veterans.
From what little information I have gathered from the veterans affairs committee, this item would give a little assistance to the unemployable. I find that in pleading the case of the unemployable, the doubtful part of it is found in the person who has to make the decision that the man is unemployable. It is generally turned back to some doctor who has no idea, beyond the medical end of it, whether a man is unemployable or not. Recently in a specific case, after a great deal of correspondence, it was finally decided that, in spite of the doctors, the man was unemployable. There was only one doctor, outside of the veterans affairs department, who would come forward, and it was on his statement that this man was awarded a pension as an unemployable. Whether he will get a further increase under this new legislation, I do not know. I have written about a man who, the department says, is not unemployable; yet it is impossible for him to make a living. He has been turned down again and again. When a man is able to work only about one day in a fortnight, I think he should be immediately classed as an unemployable.
I should have liked to hear the minister answer the question that was asked him with regard to his views on this unemployability pension. He said he did not like to speak on behalf of the government, but I took it from his remarks-

Mr. Chairman, I did not make any such statement, that I did not like to speak on behalf of the government. I said that I would not undertake to make a statement of policy on behalf of the government without first consulting with my colleagues. Let us get these facts straight.

That is right, but just the same I took it from his remarks that he was inclined to be in favour of it. I for one, Mr. Chairman, would gladly stay here until he confers with the cabinet, even if it took a day, and they change their policy, as has been suggested by the leader of the opposition. However, this item is not going to benefit anyone a great deal, having regard to the amount shown there.
The ones on behalf of whom I wish to speak are the pensioners who are now getting a starvation pension and who are not able to get any increase to keep up with the cost of living. We have all been stormed with telegrams and letters with reference to this condition, and I think it should have some consideration from the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
From time to time all members of parliament are called upon to take up the cases of veterans. I must say that lately, with regard to the last four or five cases in which I was interested, we were given complete satisfaction. In addition to living up to the letter of the law, I think the department should go a little bit further. There are many cases in which they must have compassion with reference to the man who has served overseas.
As to the comparison that was made by some other hon. members this morning when they spoke about pensions increases to other classes of civilians in order to keep up with the cost of living, may I say that to begin with we should do the same with reference to the veterans who have made application. I hope that the government will think it worth while to change their policy and will give the underpaid veteran pensioners a little break at this time.

Alberta has had an intense interest in seeing that labour is benefited in every possible way. She has undertaken a very extensive program with respect to apprentice training to enable young persons to take their place in the industrial field. In the calendar year 1950 there were thirteen conferences related to ILO, including the main meeting in June.
Is the international labour office an independent body or is it in any way associated with the United Nations?

It has a very distinct relationship with the United Nations. As my hon. friend knows, it survived the old League of Nations, came to Montreal at McGill during the war years, and then went back to Geneva. Not only is there a constant liaison between it and the United Nations, but the work of the ILO proper is under the general jurisdiction of the United Nations.
Does it have a separate budget?

Yes. By agreement signed on December 14, 1946, it was brought into official relationship with the United Nations, although retaining its identity as a separate organization. It is now one of the specialized agencies associated with the economic and social council of the United Nations.

This is not the time to be asking for long answers, but would policy matters come within its own jurisdiction, and is it to that extent an independent organization? Or is it dependent for its policy upon the larger organization?
I am going to ask my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to answer that question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend knows it much better than I. I happened to be on the committee when the relations between ILO and the United Nations were formulated in 1946 through the economic and social council. The international labour office is a tripartite body, as it represents labour, employers and government. In so far as it keeps within the purposes outlined in its statute it is a policy-making body, but as an auxiliary body of the United Nations it makes an annual report to the assembly of the United Nations.
The minister says that it is a policy-making body.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Under the economic and social council of the United Nations, which itself is an organ of the United Nations.

Is the government satisfied that its policy is sensible and' constructive, or, in plain words, that it is serving a useful purpose which would warrant our continuing to co-operate? May I say that I hope it is.

I do not think I am qualified to answer that question myself, but my deputy 80709-317J

minister has been on the governing body of ILO for a few years but never had an opportunity to attend its meetings. I insisted that he attend the main meeting in June this year, and he arrived back just a few days ago. I put exactly the same question to him, and without any hesitation he replied in the affirmative. On the basis of that, I place a good deal of importance on the work of this organization.

I should like to say a word on this - matter. I had the opportunity last year of attending the ILO conference, but it is not for that reason that I say it is a very worth-while organization. Any organization that brings employers and' workers together is worth while. In the ILO the workers are referred to as workers and not as labour. The three parts are government, employers and workers. In dealing with matters that come before the organization for consideration, the workers consider them separately by themselves and the employers do likewise. The voting is conducted separately, but when the three groups meet in general session the decision is made on the total vote of the three parts. The affirmative votes and negative votes on the three levels are taken, and the item is rejected or approved in that way. I would say it is very much worth while.

Montana, 400; maple sugar harvesters from Quebec to New England, 400; tobacco curers from the southern states to Ontario and Quebec, 1,652. I think these figures will indicate that this program is playing a very important part in making labour sufficiently mobile to be moved from one part of Canada to another in order to save the crops and harvests in the various parts of Canada.
Incidentally I think that the hon. member for Nanaimo will agree that a project such as this, which under reasonably good circumstances moves Canadians from one part of Canada to another, with an opportunity of returning to their families within a reasonable period, affords them an opportunity of better understanding the country.

Item agreed to.
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, 1942-
193. Administration, $30,431.

I would like to say a word about vote No. 193, because I was rather closely connected with the vocational training movement at the close of the last war. I have in my constituency a small but efficient school, which has a capable staff and a lot of admirable equipment. It performs a useful service in helping to maintain the motor vehicles of the various departments of government. But I feel that full advantage is not being taken of that school, and that a larger number of students could attend the school. Most of the classes deal with the maintenance* of motor vehicles, particularly those which are connected with logging and lumbering. There are also special classes to train young men in the use of the power saw and other modem lumbering appliances.
The point I want to make particularly at this moment is that it is not being used to its full capacity, and at the same time we hear that the armed services are experiencing a shortage of tradesmen. Could there not be a little closer co-ordination, as there was during the war, between this vocational training system and the training of tradesmen, as we call them, in the armed services? I should like to suggest to the minister that these classes which are now being held in these vocational training schools-I speak only with knowledge of the one in my constituency-be extended so that they could train the tradesmen who are urgently needed in the armed services.
There is one other point. I still feel that we have not given the fullest possible opportunity, even to the men who were discharged and who were taken into these training courses, to qualify themselves. I
Supply-Labour
think there was a limitation on the number of courses that they might take, but I hope that that might yet be extended.
It is with some concern that I notice there has been a general reduction of over $1 million in these three items. I would hope that further consideration might be given and, rather than reducing the activities of vocational training at this time, encouragement might be given to extension of these facilities.

I am glad that the hon. member has said that, because it is exactly what we are doing. A little later we shall come to an item in the supplementary estimates for the special purpose he has mentioned. The whole field of vocational training is being extended, even though it is not reflected in the amount of money in the main estimates. The reason for that is that there will perhaps be fewer people, due to fuller employment, available to take full-time training such as this. We are now training men on behalf of national defence, for the army and the air force. I understand that an application will be coming from that department for the navy as well, for training similar to that conducted during the last war. As the hon. member knows, the federal government pays the full amount of that training.

Is all of that
training conducted in educational institutions? How much of it is in the actual course of the practising trades?
It is all done in co-operation with the provinces, and in vocational schools.

Is all of it
conducted in that manner? I remember being through the Ford plant some time ago, and I thought I saw some people there who were- I shall not say apprentices, for perhaps that word has a technical significance-quasiapprentices. Does that mean they were practising temporarily in the plant what they had learned in school?
The Ford company has its own school.

As my colleague says, they have their own school. At the same time, in some plants such as that, the command makes arrangements direct with a plant for the training of personnel rather than doing it through these schools.
When the minister says "command"-
That is national defence.

I still think that this training is all being done in what I might call the classroom or the laboratory, and not in the factory. In other words, it does not include apprenticeship?

Supply-Labour

In the past practically all of this has been utilized in the vocational schools coming under the provinces. As a result of recommendations that have been made recently by the advisory council, we are exploring the possibility of establishing courses on the job.
May I ask to what extent apprenticeship is encouraged in the skilled trades?

To answer the hon. member briefly, I know that our advisory committee on apprenticeship which met at Ottawa not long ago, which I attended with great interest, and which represents those in that field from all the provinces as well as the federal government, is sponsoring apprenticeship training to the greatest degree possible. I have some figures here, if they would be of interest.
May I interrupt to point out that we shall need unanimous consent to resume at two o'clock instead of three o'clock after the luncheon recess. I hope that we have that consent, Mr. Chairman.
Agreed.

There is one other thing. May we have unanimous consent to rise and report progress in order to pass some minor amendments to some legislation which has come from the Senate and which the Minister of Justice is prepared to explain?

On a matter of privilege, Mr. Chairman, last evening, during the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Revenue, I made the statement that a radio station to be operated by Messrs. Stirling and Jameson at St. John's, Newfoundland, had received an allocation of steel from the Minister of Defence Production and that another vital project in which I was interested had not received an allocation. Today I am informed that that is incorrect; that not only did that station receive steel, but some three other stations received it. I am told *that the amount of steel that was given the station in St. John's was not sufficient to make one motorcar. I suggested also that the allocation was made because of the fact the station was supporting the Liberal regime. I wish to withdraw the remarks I made, as from information I received this morning, the previous information given me was incorrect.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

Mi. Gregg: I left unanswered one question when the committee rose before one o'clock, as to the development of the apprenticeship training. I think I could answer it briefly this wise. In the seven provinces with whom we have agreements there are three times as many registered for apprenticeship training as there were in 1945.
How many are there?
About 10,800. After 1945 there were two or three years in which it was inflated, owing to veterans training. Then it decreased in 1949, and since 1949 has been on the increase.
I presume these apprentices are all registered in their respective trades, are they?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, 1942-
195.	Payments to the provinces for capital expenditures for vocational schools, buildings and equipment, $1,250,000.

With respect to this item there was an appropriation of $2,250,000, in 1950-51, of which it is expected that $1,379,000 will be spent. Can the minister say why the appropriation was not used? Is it the old story of lack of building materials?

This was a building program for vocational training. It has been pretty well completed. During the years preceding there had been a very heavy program, and this was all that it was felt the provinces and the federal government needed to fill the needs.
Then we overestimated last year?
It was overestimated last year in the estimates.

Item agreed to.
Government employees compensation-
196.	Administration of the Government Employees Compensation Act, $59,716.
I notice there is a substantial increase. Will the minister say a word with regard to that?

This is to take care of the administration of the employees compensation act for those employees of Canada not under provincial government administration. The Government Employees Compensation Act, 1947, chapter 18, Statutes of Canada, 1947, which replaces the former act, chapter 30, Revised Statutes of Canada 1927, provides compensation where employees of His Majesty
Supply-Labour
are killed or suffer injuries or industrial diseases while performing their duties, at the same rate as is provided for employees of persons other than His Majesty under the law of the province in which the accidents occur, the liability for and the amount of compensation to be determined by the authority established under such law, which is usually the provincial workmen's compensation board.
I thought the minister spoke about this as applying particularly to cases outside provincial jurisdiction.
No; I was in error in giving that impression, Mr. Chairman. It applies to persons serving the federal government within provincial jurisdiction.
I understand that they are not under the provincial compensation board; nevertheless they are cases that are dealt with substantially on the same basis.
That is correct.
Are they not dealt with by the provincial board, and then this government reimburses the board?
That is right. The provincial boards act as the agent of the federal government for the purpose of the federal government employees.

Item agreed to.
Terminable services-*
199.	To provide for payment to the national film board for educational films for exhibition, $24,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am sure the minister
would be glad to hear me say that one of the films that was produced for his department that some of us saw in the railway committee room some time ago was particularly well done. I do not say that to make any comparison with the others, but I have in mind the film on labour-management co-operation. I thank the minister for arranging for members of parliament to see that film. I should like to suggest, however, that he arrange a special showing of the film for certain people who might gain from it. I have in mind the members of the civil service commission, perhaps the treasury board and deputy ministers, and all those who have to do with employee relations in the federal government service.
I will not say any more. I will simply say that I think there is room for improvement in management-labour relations in the government service, and that it might be all to the good if the people concerned saw this film.

Supply-Labour

You went so quickly over item 198 that I did not get a chance to ask a question. It has to do with vocational training for discharged members of Canada's armed forces. That has evidently reached the stage of such small compass that one wonders how the organization can be kept going at all.

Other personnel not ex-members of the armed forces are being trained in the same school. In other words the place of the veterans in the vocational schools is being taken by younger people now, and this amount is kept separate to take care of the last few veterans who are under vocational training. Of course during the coming years there will be a number of veterans, from those who come out of the armed forces that are now overseas, who will be entitled to this same training.
The same conditions will apply to those coming out as to those of world war II?
The other legislation that was put through the house during this session covers those on exactly the same terms as those of world war II.

Item agreed to.
Terminable services-
200.	To provide for expenses that may be incurred in the arranging for and the movement of workers from outside Canada to work on farms and other essential industry in Canada when Canadian labour is not available to meet the need; including costs connected with the supervision and welfare of persons already immigrated to Canada under former authorized labour movements and administrative expenses connected therewith, $667,956.

I have a couple of questions to ask. I think the minister said that 271 persons were brought to Newfoundland. Can he say what happened to them? Are they still on the island or on the mainland? Again, when he is answering on the general item, would he state how many people outside Canada were brought in this year, and if they have all remained.
It will be understood that item 200 is quite different from the one we were discussing this morning. The one we discussed this morning had reference to the movement of personnel within Canada.
I realize that.

The one we discussed this morning dealt with the federal-provincial plan to take care of harvesters, primarily. This item represents an effort the Department of Labour makes to help in moving groups of new Canadians. This is done in association with the Department of Citizenship and

Immigration. We undertake to find employment and to give the organized groups of new workers a certain amount of care while they are proceeding to their employment. I do not think that the Atlantic provinces have received many under this plan.
I realize that. I was simply asking the minister to tell me what had happened.
I believe the hon. member would like to have information with respect to those who were recruited in Newfoundland to do farm work in other parts of Canada, and what happened to them after that.
Yes; did they go back?

I do not think I can give accurate information as to what happened to them after they had completed their work. However, perhaps I can partly answer the hon. member's question by stating that last year there were 336 who came from Newfoundland into central Canada, or other parts of Canada, for agricultural purposes. Then, for track work there were 181, for mining 49, for lumbering and logging nil. Those are all for whom we have records.
There does appear to be a definite trend in moving away from the province to work in other parts of Canada. I am wondering how it will affect the province in the future.

That, of course, is an age-old question which I am sure the hon. member would not expect me to explore this afternoon. However, as he knows, in the east we are subject to seasonal unemployment. One does not look with a great deal of enthusiasm upon encouraging the exodus of Atlantic province people to the rest of Canada; nevertheless under these auspices, and with an opportunity to earn money, to take part in the development of the country, to see the rest of Canada and to go back to their own homes when their employment opens again, I think it is a much better plan than loafing around home.
Thank you. How many have been brought in from outside to work?
My colleague, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, will answer that question.
I understand the hon. member would like to know how many came from outside and went to Newfoundland.
No; to Canada generally.
During the last year 73,912 came to Canada, of whom 204 said their destination was Newfoundland.
Is there any definite amount required for the whole of Canada?

At the present time not very many, as the hon. member knows. The filling of vacancies in Newfoundland has gone on rapidly this last year. I noticed in figures I saw the other day that 58 per cent fewer people registered in our unemployment office there than there were this time last year.

I was referring to woodworkers, for whom there is a demand on the mainland of Canada. Are many being brought in for that particular trade, and are there many being brought from Newfoundland to work on the mainland? I understand there is a great demand.
We have had no requests.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration said that last year there were 204 from outside Canada who went to Newfoundland. It seems to me that moving Newfoundlanders into Ontario -
Temporarily.
Possibly so; but what I am interested in is-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Like some civil servants- temporary-permanent.
-what classifications came from outside to Newfoundland. It looks foolish to bring people in and at the same time drive them out.

A large proportion of the 204 were technicians being brought to Newfoundland by the government of the province for the purpose of increasing productive capacity and industrial capacity to absorb labour.

I notice in this item the expression, "including costs connected with the supervision and welfare of persons", and so on. There is an item for hospitalization and medical aid, which is not very large. Who assumes responsibility for these people in the event of their becoming public charges? Does the government accept responsibility for them for a certain period of time after their arrival in Canada? If so, does that come under this item.

After arrival in Canada they may call for a short period of time at one or other of the hostels. If they should be ill at that time it is the responsibility of the federal authorities. However, when they are placed in employment, in common with other Canadians, they become the responsibility of the provincial authorities.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I understand this item
includes an amount to be spent in assisting
Supply-Labour
the movement of immigrants to Canada to work in the sugar beet fields in, for example, my own province of Manitoba. If that is so, I should like to ask a question of the minister. As he knows, the question as to the welfare and continuing employment of these people has been the subject matter of some concern and even some controversy in my province. I understand federal money is expended to help bring these people over, and that it is done at the request of the Manitoba Sugar Company.
At the request of the province, so far as we are concerned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
All right, at the request of the province; but I believe it is correct to say that so far as Manitoba is concerned the province is simply passing on a request made to it by the Manitoba Sugar Company. I understand that as a rule these people are brought over at the season of the year in which they are most needed in the sugar beet fields, and that when the fall comes along and there is no further need for their services in that connection, in places where there are contracts with the Manitoba Sugar Company, these persons find themselves having to report to the employment offices in Winnipeg which come under the jurisdiction of the minister. It would seem that this does present a problem.
I quite approve the policy of aiding immigration to this country, particularly when it is on a selective basis or when it is on humanitarian grounds. But it does seem to me that, if we are going to spend federal money assisting a company like the Manitoba Sugar Company to get over here employees whom they need, that company has some responsibility to see to it that these people are continued in employment and not thrown back on the various governments when the company has no further need for them. In the spring the company may want them back. If the company is going to act that way I do not think they should get any financial assistance from the public. On the other hand, if we do provide assistance I suggest that some responsibility rests upon the company. I should be glad to have some comment from the minister on this matter.

I know of the matter to which my hon. friend refers. We have had no serious complaints from those brought in or from the municipal authorities that people had been left on their hands. The information I have had so far is that after they are through working for the sugar beet company, in the main they find employment in some other field of activity. I shall be glad to look into the matter during the recess.

Supply-Labour

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, they come to the minister's officials to ask for employment. It would not appear to be accepted as the responsibility of the company, despite the fact that they have had a definite form of assistance.	.
They come to the national employment service to see what openings there are, just the same as other Canadians who might be seeking employment anywhere in Canada.
Has there been any request for outside labour in connection with the development on the north shore of the St. Lawrence at Seven Islands?	-
No.

Following the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the minister stated that so far there had been no protests from the municipalities. I do not suppose any municipality would protest if only a small measure of assistance was being required. The fact is that we have been going through a period of fairly full employment. These seasonal employees are being quite readily absorbed, but I am thinking of the situation which caused' me to make some extended remarks when we were discussing the unemployment insurance regulations earlier in the session. If we had even a minor recession many of these people would become a definite charge upon the municipality, because the provinces do not enter into the picture. I do not want to speak at any length on this matter, but I feel we must take this question under consideration.

Item agreed to.
Unemployment Insurance Act. 1940-
201.	Administration, including expenditures incurred in connection with the activities of the national employment service as delegated by the Minister of Labour in accordance with section 88 of the act, $23,847,199.

When, the unemployment insurance advisory committee reported for the year ending March 31, 1950, they stated:
The committee has considered the advisability of Instituting a new actuarial investigation.
After remarking that the time for this *eemed inopportune, they went on to say:
The committee does intend, however, to have partial investigations made on the basis of information on a sample of contributors from which it hopes to obtain guidance in its future recommendations.
Can the minister say whether any progress has been made along that line?

The report has not finally been dealt with, but is being carefully considered. I have nothing to report on that as yet.
iMr. Gregg.]

There is another point I should like to bring up in connection with the unemployment insurance commission, the unemployment insurance advisory committee and any other committees which may be set up. I notice that item 714 of the supplementary estimates refers to an advisory committee. Some time ago I asked for information with respect to the number of male and female employees in the unemployment insurance commission. I find that there are 3,900 male and approximately 3,000 female employees. As all hon. members know, there is a large female labour force in the country.
Without attempting at all to upset the present standing of the commission, I suggest to the minister that if and when there is a vacancy consideration should be given to the appointment of a woman.. If there is no prospect of a change in the near future, I suggest that a woman be appointed as an additional commissioner. I suggest also that there be a woman member on the unemployment insurance advisory committee. I think it goes without saying that no one understands the problems of women workers better than a woman, and I believe the large female labour force should have representation on each of these bodies.

Under the present statute one member of the unemployment insurance commission is appointed after consultation with the national labour organization; one member is appointed after consultation with the national employer organization, and the chairman is appointed by the government. I shall be glad to give consideration to the suggestions of the hon. member. I think our advisory committees generally have woman members.

It might be difficult to
enlarge the commission when it is appointed in that way. I know a commission may be, made unwieldy because of persons appointed to represent specific segments of the population; nevertheless these problems present themselves from time to time for and on behalf of women, and I think there should be a woman commissioner.
Has the minister considered the payment of allowances for sickness?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before the minister answers perhaps I may be permitted to say a word. I suggest that along with the study of annuity matters that the minister told us this morning was to be made between now and the time parliament meets again, he might also consider amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act to extend the coverage, at least under certain circumstances, to periods of illness.
The minister knows from debates that have taken place in former sessions that

some of us, the hon. member for Vancouver East and I in particular, have emphasized how unfair we feel it is, and how unfair the workers feel it is, that a worker on unemployment insurance, because there is no work for him, is cut off benefits if he happens to take ill, even though there is still no work for him. There are still wider changes that some of us might advocate, but it seems to me this is an immediate request that should be met, namely that when a worker goes on benefits and qualifies for them in the usual way, he should not have those benefits cut off because he takes ill. It has happened to a good many workers who have been on benefits and have not known of this regulation that on a certain day of the week when they were supposed to report they have sent their wives to collect the benefits and the wife is asked where her husband is. She says that he is at home ill, and immediately he is cut off unemployment insurance benefit, at a time when he needs it more than ever, despite the fact that there is still no job for him.
We have developed that argument so fully in previous debates that I do not need to go into it in detail now, but I say hopefully that I trust the minister will give the matter very active study during the recess. When he consults his departmental officials on the matter I am sure he will find that it has been studied by his officials and there must be quite a body of material on it.
One other supporting argument I should like to make is that away back in the November, 1944, issue of "Canadian Affairs", a pamphlet put out by the wartime information board which was sent mainly to the troops overseas to tell them what was going on back home, this question was dealt with as follows:
Unemployment Insurance only covers the worker who has lost a job and is still available for employment. If you are sick, you aren't available for employment-so you don't get unemployment insurance. Once health insurance is finally put into operation, it probably won't be long until the Unemployment Insurance Act is amended to provide for payment of benefits during the period of a workman's illness. If that happens then a worker off for sickness would get unemployment insurance sickness benefit to make up for lost wages and would have his medical and hospital expenses met out of the health insurance fund-to which he has been contributing.
I recognize that we have not yet the health insurance which that very pamphlet forecast as something to be expected in the near future. But I suggest that if the Department of National Health and Welfare is too slow in proceeding with health insurance, the Minister of Labour might give a lead in this field by bringing in the kind of amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act that was
Supply-Labour
forecast in that "Canadian Affairs" pamphlet sent overseas to the troops in November, 1944.
I need not go into the matter further, because the records of Hansard are full of arguments on the point. In this corner of the house we have felt at times that we had sufficiently made our point to hope that the amendment would be forthcoming soon. I hope the minister's study between now and the fall will bear fruit.
I can assure my hon. friend of a study at least.

I should like to point out that considerable study is necessary on the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. For example, in many industries the worker pays into a sick benefit fund. He pays for that insurance against a time of unemployment because of sickness. At the same time he contributes to the unemployment insurance fund which provides for benefits during a period of unemployment. When the worker takes ill he is entitled to collect the insurance for which he has been paying because he is not able to carry on his regular work. The sick benefit that he draws amounts to perhaps ten per cent of what his normal wages would be. Under the circumstances, with the worker away from work because of sickness and collecting insurance that he has paid for, I think he is also legitimately entitled to receive unemployment insurance benefits for which he has already paid, because he is only receiving about ten per cent of his normal wages.
I refer particularly to the steel and coal industries in my part of the country. The worker is placed in the position that if he applies for unemployment insurance under the circumstances I have described, the company will immediately take the stand that he has severed his connection with them as an employee, and his pension rights are affected. He has a pension plan, and if he ceases his employment then he loses his pension rights.
This subject has been a controversial one for a number of years in my part of the country. I am questioned about it all the time. I think the worker is entitled to the unemployment insurance for which he has paid. I think he is entitled to collect the sick benefit insurance for which he has paid. I am asked whether a man should apply for unemployment insurance, and I have to warn him that if he does, it is taken as an indication that he has severed his connection with the company, that he is no longer an employee, and that he will lose out on the pension scheme in which he has participated to protect his future.

Supply-Labour
There has been a lot of wrangling about the matter. When the minister is making an analysis of the problem, I think something should be done to correct the situation. In the first place the worker is entitled to the sickness insurance for which he has paid, and which amounts to about ten per cent of his earnings. Second, the worker is entitled to collect unemployment insurance benefits, because he has already paid for them. Some understanding should be reached also with these large companies that a worker's pension rights will not be affected if he applies for unemployment insurance under circumstances such as I have described.

Item agreed to.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940-
202.	Government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, $27,500,000.
I take it that the government's contribution is larger because total wages for the year are larger?
And a larger working force generally.
What is the total now at the credit of the fund, and how is it invested?
How does that compare with a year ago?
As of March 31, 1950, the total was $582,646,972.52. The figure for 1951 is also as of March 31. The investments are all in either Canadian government or Canadian National Railway bonds.
Would the minister read those figures again?

Just the
millions.
$664 million in 1951, $582 million in 1950, and $529 million in 1949.

I was a little surprised, considering the fact there was a period of rather full employment, that notwithstanding the additional contribution of some $25 million the fund has gone down something over $80 million.
No, it has gone up. I gave the 1951 figure first.

Then I
reverse my surprise and express my surprise that it has gone up so much.

That is because of the full
employment.
In the report it refers to contributions paid other than by stamp. Would that mean through the use of meters or some other form of contribution to the fund?
Meter machines or bulk payments by cheque.
But it is all by contributions?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
204. To provide for the payment of unemployment assistance to certain residents of Newfoundland to give effect to the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada, in accordance with regulations of the governor in council and such assistance shall be deemed to be a benefit or payment within the meaning of sections 33 and 67 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, $500,000.

There is a great difference, Mr. Chairman, between the amount provided this year, $500,000, and the amount provided last year, which was $4 million. Can the minister fell me why there is that big drop?

This is strictly in accord with the union agreement. As the hon. member will recall, it was felt that there would be a great deal of unemployment after union, and this measure was adopted as a means of taking up that slack over the first few years.
I understand it now. Would the minister be able to tell me whether any consideration has been given to providing unemployment insurance for fishermen? Has any progress been made in that regard?
Yes, the report is now being studied.
Does it appear to be favourable?
Answer next session.

Item agreed to.
707. Departmental administration-further amount required, $13,057.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is at least one matter under item 707 which I should like to draw to the minister's attention. I want to be sure he has plenty of homework to do between now and the fall session. I would urge him to study a number of items in the briefs presented to the government this year by the labour congresses, but for the moment I am concentrating on one. It is to be found on page 15 of the memorandum presented to the government of Canada by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada on April 10, 1951. The paragraph reads as follows:
Another very important and necessary amendment that we seek-

The reference is to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.

speechtext: This deals with transportation of mail, and gives me an opportunity to remind the minister that on several occasions I have taken up the case of the men known as the postal couriers who drive the trucks in the city of Winnipeg that pick up the mail from the letter boxes and transport it between stations, to trains and so on. [DOT]

membership in the House of Commons I have found invariably that the estimates of the Minister of Finance are completed as almost the last order of business at the end of the session, when everyone is tired and anxious to get away-and let me add that I am just as tired and anxious to get away as anyone else.

I propose to ask five questions, and I shall ask the Minister of Finance, with his experts, to answer these questions. I have sent copies of them to the parliamentary assistant who, by the way, is left to carry the burden alone at this time. For some reason or other, the Minister of Finance is away.
